prize_parts.citation: For a visionary Romanian prose oeuvre, rooted in poetry, that builds vast inner cosmologies from memory, the body and dream in densely patterned long forms.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize part for Mircea Cărtărescu (B026). The configuration holds, but the citation wording has changed after the exchange. I now anchor it on the prose and name poetry as a root, not as a co-equal pillar. The chair's round-2 question on scope pushed me there. My round-1 wording treated the poetry as the base of the project, and I have since called that a hypothesis I cannot verify. Carlberg's proposal is the more honest basis for a whole-oeuvre citation, and I adopt it. The literary case rests on the criteria I stated in round 1. His voice is recognizable as no one else's, in the sense of 'a voice I find in this particular writer's work and nowhere else'. The formal achievement is the construction of very large, patterned structures in the Blinding (Orbitor) sequence and Solenoid, which are built and not merely long. The imaginative and intellectual depth lies in treating memory, the body and metaphysical speculation as one enterprise. The oeuvre looks consolidated, so I do not see premature judgment as the issue. This is a judgment from general public knowledge and the colleagues' stated views, not from independently verified reading. Round 1 gave me no answer to the depth-versus-excess question, and I do not claim to have settled it. I weigh it as the main risk to the case, not as a reason to move. On Can Xue and Carson, my two alternatives, the exchange did not supply what would lift either above Cărtărescu. For Can Xue the missing evidence is variation across a largely untranslated corpus. For Carson it is a citation scope that separates original work from scholarship, translation and design-dependent books. The agreement on B026 is not evidence of merit, and I do not treat it as such.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and is the same one every colleague named. The achievement lives in dense, rhythmic Romanian prose that I can judge only through translation, so how much patterning and musicality survives is beyond me. Whether the maximalist, digressive long forms are architecture or accumulation is the real test, and no one in round 1 gave specific, work-level evidence either way. Palm's formulation is the right one: do the long novels deepen their image systems or only recirculate them? If later volumes mostly extend earlier image systems, my claim of sustained quality across the whole oeuvre weakens. Sward's point also stands. If the committee weighted reinvention of a language or genre above expansion of an established visionary mode, Adonis or Tawada would have a stronger claim than I currently credit. I cannot assess either in the original, and that limit is on my judgment, not a verdict on the work.

responses.point: Carlberg proposes anchoring the Cărtărescu citation on the novels, with poetry as the origin of the vision and not an independently assessed pillar, because translated coverage of the poetry is thin. She also keeps Can Xue as a close alternative on rigor-versus-repetition grounds.
responses.response: I accept the anchoring and have rewritten my citation accordingly. It answers a question I raised myself in round 1: the poetry-as-base claim is the part I can least verify. A citation that names the prose project and mentions poetry only as its root claims no more than we can weigh. On Can Xue, I agree that the open rigor-versus-repetition question, together with partial translation, is what separates her from Cărtărescu for me. I would add that this is a gap in the evidence available to us, not a demonstrated gap in achievement. That is why she stays my first alternative and not a dismissed candidate.

responses.point: Palm proposes a concrete test of Cărtărescu's long forms: whether the late novels deepen their image systems or only recirculate them. She cites a visible arc from the poetry through the Blinding sequence to Solenoid, and says she cannot judge whether a comparable arc exists for Can Xue given partial translation.
responses.response: I accept the test and the symmetry. The same question should be asked of Cărtărescu and of Can Xue, and neither can be answered from reputation alone. I would qualify one point. The arc Palm sees from poetry to the Blinding sequence to Solenoid is persuasive as a public-record observation about progression, but part of it is inferred from partial translation of the earlier work, as she acknowledges. So I treat it as supporting evidence and not as proof. What does move me is the shift in scale and organization between the Blinding sequence and Solenoid, which suggests development in form and not repetition of method. I keep that as a judgment from public knowledge and not a verified reading. It is enough to keep my preference, not enough to treat the question as closed.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Can Xue eighth because he cannot tell whether four decades of consistent method amount to deepening or restatement, and he allows that readers of the originals might see more development. He also treats Carson's scope as the decisive weakness, because her books depend on physical design and her cumulative weight is hard to establish.
responses.response: I share your uncertainty about Can Xue and I think your caveat about readers of the Chinese is the fairest statement of it. My difference is one of weighting. A consistent method is not itself an absence of development, but I cannot show development from the corpus available to me, so I do not rank her above Cărtărescu. On Carson I agree that scope decides the matter. I would add that the issue is not whether the work is literature, since the writing is clearly literature. The issue is whether a citation can be written around her original poetry, verse narrative and essays alone and still describe a whole body of work. Round 1 gives me no basis to say yes with confidence, so she remains a second alternative.

responses.point: Sward says that if the committee valued reinvention of a language or genre over expansion of an established visionary mode, Tawada or Adonis would have a stronger claim than Cărtărescu. She does not hold this as her preference but flags it as a different weighting of the common criteria.
responses.response: This is the strongest challenge to my position and I do not want to wave it away. I do think Cărtărescu's achievement is more than expansion of a known mode. A work organized on that scale around memory and the body is itself a formal construction, and I would not reduce it to a period label. But I cannot rule out that a reader with Arabic, or with both Japanese and German, would find a more radical transformation of a poetic language than I can see. I read the limit as mine. It is also why I will not argue that the Cărtărescu case is stronger on criteria I cannot test for Adonis or Tawada. My claim is only that, on the evidence I can actually weigh, his case is the most fully demonstrable.

responses.point: Olsson, as chair, asks whether the committee can separate public political positions from the literary case for every candidate, and he treats the durability of the longest works as something reputation cannot settle. He also says that if a Carson citation could be defined around original poetic work he would take it more seriously.
responses.response: I agree on keeping politics out of the literary case for all candidates, and I would apply it to the Cărtărescu citation as well: no representative-of-a-region framing. On durability, I accept that reputation cannot decide it and that my reliance on public knowledge is a limit I cannot remove here. On Carson, your conditional is fair. If the scope were drawn around the original written work, I would regard her as a serious claim, which is why she stays among my alternatives. Even then, the weight of short and fragmentary forms against a large sustained project remains unresolved for me.

uncertainties: How much of the density, rhythm and musicality of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose survives translation, and whether the longest novels deepen their image systems or recirculate them. I have not settled this from public knowledge.
How much of the poetry and early work is available in translation. I treat poetry as a root of the prose project and not as an independently assessed pillar of the citation.
Whether Can Xue's consistent method over a very large, partly translated output shows development or restatement. This is a limit of the evidence available to me, not a finding about her work.
Whether a Carson citation can be confined to original poetry, verse narrative and essays, and whether short or fragmentary books carry enough cumulative weight for a lifetime citation.
For Adonis and Tawada, whether a reader of the originals would find a stronger case for transformation of a language than I can see, given that wordplay and prosody are what translation loses first.
The record is limited to my profile, the shortlist and the round-1 files. I have not read the corpus for this exercise or independently verified any bibliography or translation coverage.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-relevant connection to any shortlisted writer is apparent from my supplied profile. Documented connections are to committee colleagues and to the Gothenburg and West Sweden press. My own historical and dream-logic fiction, and my reading of dream-logic and long-form prose, is context only and is not evidence of a preference for any candidate. This is disclosed and not adjudicated.
